title: Linear & Simultaneous Equations
summary:
A **linear equation** is one where the unknown appears only to the first power (no squares, no roots) — its graph is a straight line. Solving one is pure rearrangement: collect the unknown on one side, the numbers on the other, then divide by its coefficient. To solve $2(x+3) = 14$: expand or divide first ($x + 3 = 7$), then subtract ($x = 4$).

**Straight-line form.** Most linear relationships are written $y = mx + c$, where $m$ is the **gradient** (slope — how fast $y$ rises per unit $x$) and $c$ is the **intercept** (the value of $y$ when $x = 0$). Recognising this form lets you read a graph or a data trend instantly, and it appears constantly in energy work — calibration lines, cost-vs-output, linear approximations.

**Simultaneous equations** come up whenever two unknowns are tied together by two conditions — two prices, two flows, a mix of two streams. You need *as many equations as unknowns*. There are two standard methods.

**Substitution** works best when one equation already gives a variable on its own. From $y = 2x$ and $x + y = 12$: substitute the first into the second, $x + 2x = 12 \Rightarrow 3x = 12 \Rightarrow x = 4$, then back-substitute $y = 8$.

**Elimination** works best when adding or subtracting the equations cancels a variable. For $x + y = 10$ and $x - y = 4$: **add** them and the $y$'s cancel, $2x = 14 \Rightarrow x = 7$, then $y = 3$. If the coefficients don't match, scale one (or both) equations first so that one variable has equal-and-opposite (or equal) coefficients, then add (or subtract).

The universal recipe: (1) count unknowns and make sure you have that many equations; (2) pick substitution (a variable is already isolated) or elimination (adding/subtracting will cancel one); (3) solve for one variable; (4) back-substitute for the other; (5) check both original equations. Geometrically, the solution is the single point where the two straight lines cross.

equations.name: Linear equation — solve
equations.useWhen: The unknown appears once, to the first power. Undo the +/− then the ×/÷ (reverse BIDMAS) to isolate it.
equations.note: Expand brackets, or divide the whole equation by the bracket's multiplier first — either is valid.

equations.name: Straight line
equations.useWhen: Describing or reading any linear relationship. $m$ is the gradient (rise per unit run); $c$ is where the line meets the $y$-axis ($x=0$).
equations.note: Two points give the gradient $m = \Delta y/\Delta x$; one point plus $m$ gives $c$.

equations.name: Simultaneous — elimination
rearrangements: \text{add the equations: } y \text{ cancels} \Rightarrow x = 7, \; y = 3
equations.useWhen: Adding or subtracting the two equations will cancel a variable. Scale one or both first if the coefficients don't already match.
equations.note: Add when a variable has equal-and-opposite signs; subtract when it has equal signs.

equations.name: Simultaneous — substitution
equations.useWhen: One equation already gives a variable by itself (or is easy to rearrange to). Put that expression into the other equation to leave one unknown.
equations.note: Always back-substitute to find the second variable, and check both original equations.

glossary.definition: An equation whose unknown appears only to the first power (no $x^2$, $\sqrt{x}$, etc.). Its graph is a straight line and it has a single solution.
The $m$ in $y = mx + c$: how much $y$ changes per unit increase in $x$, $m = \Delta y/\Delta x$. Steeper line = larger gradient.
The $c$ in $y = mx + c$: the value of $y$ where the line crosses the $y$-axis (i.e. when $x = 0$).
The number multiplying a variable. Removing it (by dividing) is the last step in isolating the unknown.
Two (or more) equations that must hold at once, linking the same unknowns. You need as many independent equations as unknowns.
Solve one equation for a variable, then put that expression into the other, leaving a single-variable equation to solve.
Add or subtract the equations (after scaling if needed) so one variable cancels, leaving a single-variable equation.
Once you have one variable, put its value into an original equation to find the other. Always finish by checking both equations.

tips: **Linear = unknown to the first power only.** No squares or roots — so the solution is a single value, found by plain rearrangement.
**Read $y = mx + c$ on sight:** $m$ is the slope (rise per run), $c$ is the start value at $x=0$. Most calibration and cost lines are in this form.
**Match the method to the equations.** Use substitution when a variable is already isolated; use elimination when adding/subtracting will cancel one.
**To eliminate, make coefficients match.** Multiply an equation through so one variable has equal (subtract) or equal-and-opposite (add) coefficients, then combine.
**Always back-substitute and check.** Find the second variable, then verify your pair satisfies *both* original equations — it catches sign slips.
**You need as many equations as unknowns.** Two unknowns need two independent equations; one equation alone can't pin down both.
